title: Psalm 88: Darkness Is My Closest Companion
summary: A man who has suffered since his youth cries to God day and night from the edge of death. He feels God's wrath sweeping over him like waves, his friends have turned from him, and he asks whether the dead can praise God. The psalm never turns to confidence or thanks; it ends with the words that darkness is his closest companion.
story: Psalm 88 is the bleakest prayer in the Psalter, and it stands in a telling place. It comes right after Psalm 87's joyful vision of the nations enrolled in Zion and right before Psalm 89, which praises God's covenant with David and then mourns its apparent collapse. Book III as a whole traces Israel's descent into national disaster, and Psalm 88 gives that descent a single human voice. Almost every lament in the Psalms turns somewhere toward trust or praise; this one does not. Yet it is still addressed to "the God of my salvation" (verse 1), and it was kept, sung, and handed down by the worshiping community. Its presence in Scripture tells the reader that there are seasons of faith in which the only thing left is to keep speaking to God.
historical:
The heading is the longest and most layered in the Psalter. It calls the psalm a song, a psalm of the sons of Korah, for the choirmaster, according to Mahalath Leannoth, and a Maskil of Heman the Ezrahite. Heman appears in Chronicles as one of the three chief Levitical singers David appointed, alongside Asaph and Ethan (1 Chronicles 15:19), and 1 Kings 4:31 names a Heman among the famous wise men whom Solomon surpassed. Whether these are the same person is debated. The double attribution, to the Korahite guild and to Heman, may mean the psalm belonged to both, or that two headings have been combined. Maskil is a term of uncertain meaning, perhaps a skillful or instructive poem. Mahalath Leannoth may name a tune; mahalath also occurs in the heading of Psalm 53, and leannoth may relate to the verb to afflict, but no one knows for certain.

The psalm gives no historical event. It describes a lifelong affliction ("From my youth I was afflicted and near death", verse 15), and some interpreters have suggested a chronic illness, possibly one like the skin diseases that required isolation under the law (Leviticus 13:45-46), since the speaker says he is repulsive to his friends and confined. Others read the psalm as a national lament voiced by an individual, perhaps from the period of the exile. The text allows both.
cultural:
Most Old Testament texts picture death as descent into Sheol, the realm of the dead beneath the earth, also called the Pit, the grave, Abaddon (a word related to the verb to perish), the darkness, and "the land of oblivion" (verse 12). The dead in Sheol are pictured as shadowy shades, weak and cut off from the life of worship. For an Israelite, the great loss of death was not only the end of earthly life but separation from the community that praised God in the temple. That is the force of the psalmist's questions in verses 10 to 12: if he dies, he can no longer declare God's loving devotion among the living. Only in a few places does the Old Testament speak clearly of resurrection (Isaiah 26:19; Daniel 12:2), and Psalm 88 speaks from before that hope is spelled out.

Illness and social isolation went together in the ancient world. A person with a visible or unclean disease could be kept outside the camp or the town, cut off from family and worship. Friends might withdraw not only from fear of contagion but because suffering was widely assumed to be a sign of divine displeasure, the assumption Job's friends make. Spreading out one's hands (verse 9) was the ordinary posture of prayer.
literary: Psalm 88 is an individual lament, but it lacks the turn to confidence, the vow of praise, or the thanksgiving that almost every other lament contains. It is built from three cries, each marked by a time of day or a posture: "day and night I cry out" (verse 1), "I call to You daily" (verse 9), and "in the morning my prayer comes before You" (verse 13). After each cry comes a complaint. The first (verses 3 to 8) describes the speaker as already among the dead and names God as the one who has put him there. The second (verses 10 to 12) is a series of six rhetorical questions about whether God is praised among the dead. The third (verses 14 to 18) asks why God rejects him and hides his face. Images of darkness and water recur throughout: the depths, the waves, the flood that engulfs him. The psalm ends not on a period of hope but on the word darkness.

outline.t: A cry to the God of salvation
Counted among the dead, overwhelmed by God's wrath
Why do you hide your face? Darkness remains

doctrines.note: The psalm refuses easy explanations for suffering. It does not claim the speaker deserved it or that relief is near. It simply brings unrelieved pain before God, and Scripture preserves that prayer as a faithful one.
Even when there is nothing left but complaint, the speaker keeps praying, day and night and in the morning. The psalm teaches that honest protest addressed to God is itself an act of faith.

Hope in this psalm is almost invisible, held only in the address "God of my salvation" and in the act of continuing to pray. The questions about the dead also press toward a hope the Old Testament later states more fully: that God's power reaches even into death.

words.note: Sheol, the realm of the dead. In most Old Testament texts it is the place all the dead go, righteous and wicked alike, pictured as a dark underworld. It is not the same as the later idea of hell as a place of punishment. Here it represents the threat of total separation from the life and worship of God's people.

Abaddon, destruction, from the verb to perish. It appears in poetry as a name for the realm of the dead (Job 26:6; Proverbs 15:11). In Revelation 9:11 the name is given to the angel of the abyss. In verse 11 it is the place where the psalmist fears God's faithfulness can no longer be proclaimed.

Yeshuah, salvation. The word appears only once in the psalm, in its first line: "the God of my salvation". Everything after it seems to contradict it, and yet the speaker never withdraws it. The whole prayer is spoken to the God who saves, even when he seems absent.

christ: The New Testament does not quote Psalm 88, so any connection to Christ is thematic, not a claimed fulfillment. But Christians have long read it alongside the passion of Jesus, and the church has often prayed it on Good Friday and Holy Saturday. The Gospels show Jesus in the psalm's condition: abandoned by his friends (Mark 14:50), numbered with transgressors, cut off from the land of the living, and crying out on the cross from darkness to the God who seemed to have forsaken him (Mark 15:33-34). The psalmist asks whether God works wonders for the dead and whether departed spirits rise up to praise him. The resurrection is the New Testament's answer: in raising Jesus, God did a wonder among the dead, and the one who went down to the grave rose to praise him in the assembly (compare Hebrews 2:12, which quotes Psalm 22 of the risen Christ). The psalm does not know that answer, and it is important to let it speak without it. But its question is the one the gospel answers.

hard.q: Why is there a psalm in the Bible that ends with no hope at all?
hard.a:
Psalm 88 is unique in the Psalter for never turning from complaint to confidence, and readers are right to be troubled by it. Several answers have been given. Many pastors and interpreters see it as a gift to sufferers: it shows that God's people can bring even despair to him without first tidying it up, and that such prayers are not faithless. The psalmist speaks to God, not merely about him, and calls him the God of his salvation. Faith here looks like persistence rather than feeling.

Others read the psalm within the Psalter as a whole. It is not the last word; it sits in a book that ends in praise, and the reader is meant to hold it together with the psalms around it rather than alone. Still others note that its questions about death press toward the resurrection hope that later Scripture makes clearer. These answers work together. None of them removes the darkness from the psalm, and the psalm does not ask to have it removed. It asks to be heard.

questions: Psalm 88 keeps praying even though nothing changes. What does it look like to keep speaking to God when you feel nothing in return?
The speaker's friends have turned away from him. How can a church stay present with someone whose suffering doesn't resolve?
Why do you think the people of God preserved and sang a psalm that ends in darkness? What would be lost if it were not in the Bible?
